doc.title: Al Gafa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 2, 2023

title: Influences of Johnny Smith and Wes Montgomery
summary: He admired Smith's sound and voicings but was more influenced by Wes Montgomery, heard in Harlem.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: I think I read that Johnny Smith was an influence on you when you first started playing. Is that correct?

Yeah it was. I loved the sound that he got, I loved the voicings that he got, and I wanted to try to figure out how to do both. The technique I could do, the voicings, my fingers were not as long as his were and not — yeah. I worked — I got one part of it but not both parts. And so I used to listen to him so much that if I bought a new album I could tell you what he was going to play before he even played it, and where he was going to play. I

could just hear it you know. He was definitely an influence in that part of my career. But the other influence on me was Wes Montgomery. I used to go to, there was a club in Harlem called “Count Basie’s.” They used to feature guitar trios: guitar, organ and drums. And it was loaded with really good players, Wes, Kenny Burrell, Grant Green, George Benson, and a saxophone player named Eddie Harris. So I go in to listen to Wes and I’d listen from ten to two in the morning. Then I’d drive home and I’d practice another three hours or so. Because he just, he was so inspiring and he played so wonderful ideas I wanted to find out, before I forgot them I wanted to see if I could find them. And I spent many nights over there sitting on a bar stool listening and hearing this guy play. It was just fire, fire, beauty. And I think he was a more influential on my career than Johnny Smith because I kind of gravitated to the thicker sound and the triplets would come out a little different than Johnny Smith’s triplets. So I loved him. And when he died it was a loss for me you know. His career had just started to change into the Creed Taylor years where it started to change. And it was not the same Wes that I was listening to but it was still really good anyway.
Yeah I think some people, maybe it was Creed, saw a new avenue for him and maybe more sales.

Absolutely more sales. And you know what? Wes was such a great guy that he deserved anything that he could get financially from his success. He was just — he’d see you on the street — the first time I saw him on the street I didn’t even know him. I’m walking in one direction and he’s walking the other way. And he says hi. So that’s — I know other guys that would look at you and say what are you looking at, and that kind of thing you know. So Wes was just a magnificent person.
